relations.note: They are paired pedagogically as Indigenous heroines transformed into regional flowers.

god_relations.note: In some modern variants, Anahí sings or prays to Tupã, who hears her.
Some modern variants say Tupã transforms Anahí into the ceibo.
Tupá pities the drowned lover and changes her or him into irupé.

Akãhatã.note: Akãhatã is the rival warrior opposing the lovers.

I-Cuñá-Payé.note: Morotí enters the Paraná to recover Pitá from her enchantment.

Jaci.myth: Jaci makes Naiá the star of waters
Jaci.note: In the Brazilian cognate, Jaci transforms the drowned heroine into vitória-régia.

Jasy.myth: The maiden pursues the Moon’s reflection
Jasy.note: The moon-lover seeks Jasy, embraces its reflection, and drowns.

Mburucuyá heroine.note: Both belong to the literary genre linking Indigenous heroines with flowers.

Morotí.myth: Morotí and Pitá become the irupé
Morotí.note: Morotí’s transformed body forms the flower’s white inner petals.

Naiá.note: Naiá occupies the corresponding Brazilian heroine role but is not identical historically.

Panambí.note: Panambí loves Irupé and imagines becoming a butterfly to caress her.

Paraná.note: The personified river courts and embraces Irupé as its vegetable bride.

Paraná.myth: The river creates its vegetable bride
Paraná.note: The personified Paraná supplies the agency for the maiden’s floral transformation.

Pitá.myth: Morotí and Pitá become the irupé
Pitá.note: Irupé’s Morotí incarnation loves Pitá and joins him in the flower.
